Source scope and methods.statement: The ADA Standards of Care chapter provides current clinical practice recommendations on glycemic assessment, individualized glycemic goals, hypoglycemia, intercurrent illness, and hyperglycemic-crisis prevention and outpatient management.

The ADA Professional Practice Committee updates the Standards of Care annually or more frequently as warranted; the detailed evidence-grading system and development methodology are delegated to the separate Introduction and Methodology.
Contributor duality-of-interest information is provided separately through the ADA disclosure document at DOI 10.2337/dc26-SDIS.

Conditions affecting red blood cell turnover, including anemia, glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency, recent transfusion, erythropoiesis-stimulating drugs, kidney failure, and pregnancy, can interfere with A1C accuracy.
A1C does not directly measure glycemic variability, real-time glucose, or hypoglycemia.
Race and ethnicity should not be used as considerations for how A1C is applied clinically for glycemic monitoring.
Fructosamine and glycated albumin reflect glycemia over approximately 2–4 weeks and may be useful alternatives when A1C interpretation is problematic or A1C cannot be measured.
The evidence base for fructosamine and glycated albumin as glycemic-monitoring biomarkers is much weaker than the evidence base for A1C because few clinical trials have evaluated them.
High glucose coefficient of variation above 36% has been associated with occurrence of hypoglycemia.
Two retrospective studies reported that TIR above 70% aligns approximately with A1C around 7%.

For older adults with complex/intermediate health using CGM, a practical target is at least 50% TIR (12 hours/day), no more than 1% TBR below 70 mg/dL (15 minutes/day), with more permissive hyperglycemia up to 50% of the day if needed to prevent hypoglycemia.
Postprandial glucose should generally be measured 1–2 hours after the beginning of a meal when postprandial assessment is needed.

The chapter interprets the curvilinear A1C–microvascular relationship to mean that the largest absolute complication reduction occurs when very high A1C is lowered to moderate levels; further lowering from 7% to 6% yields smaller absolute benefit and may be outweighed by hypoglycemia risk when using hypoglycemia-causing therapy.

ADVANCE and VADT reported modest nephropathy reductions with intensive glycemic management, while ACCORD was stopped after a median 3.5 years because mortality was higher in the intensive-treatment arm.

For people with type 2 diabetes and established CVD, kidney disease, heart failure, and/or obesity, the chapter emphasizes use of SGLT2 inhibitors and/or GLP-1–based therapies with demonstrated organ benefits independent of current A1C, individualized A1C goal, or metformin therapy.
CGM clinical trials are described as reducing hypoglycemia rates in insulin-treated populations, while CGM can reveal asymptomatic hypoglycemia and warn of falling glucose.

For most hypoglycemia episodes in conscious people, the chapter advises 15 g carbohydrate; users of automated insulin delivery typically need 5–10 g unless exercise-related hypoglycemia or substantial meal-bolus overestimation is present.
People taking acarbose should use pure glucose rather than sucrose-containing carbohydrate for hypoglycemia treatment because acarbose inhibits sucrose breakdown.
People at risk for DKA should check ketones when symptoms or precipitating factors are present, particularly when glucose exceeds 200 mg/dL (11.1 mmol/L).
People using intensive insulin therapy should not stop basal insulin even when not eating; individualized illness/fasting dose-adjustment instructions are needed to prevent DKA.

Assessment of glycemic status.statement: Recommendation 6.1a: Assess glycemic status by A1C.
Recommendation 6.1b: Assess glycemic status using CGM metrics such as time in range, time above range, and time below range when appropriate.
Recommendation 6.1c: Fructosamine or CGM can be used for glycemic monitoring when an alternative to A1C is required.

Recommendation 6.2: Assess glycemic status at least twice yearly and more frequently, such as every 3 months, when goals are not met, treatment changes occur, frequent or severe hypo- or hyperglycemia occurs, health status changes, or children/adolescents are in rapid growth and development.
A1C reflects average glycemia over approximately 2–3 months and is the primary glycemic-status assessment tool in clinical practice and trials.
Table 6.1 maps A1C 5% (31 mmol/mol) to estimated average glucose 97 mg/dL (95% CI 76–120) or 5.4 mmol/L (95% CI 4.2–6.7).
Table 6.1 maps A1C 6% (42 mmol/mol) to estimated average glucose 126 mg/dL (95% CI 100–152) or 7.0 mmol/L (95% CI 5.5–8.5).
Table 6.1 maps A1C 7% (53 mmol/mol) to estimated average glucose 154 mg/dL (95% CI 123–185) or 8.6 mmol/L (95% CI 6.8–10.3).
Table 6.1 maps A1C 8% (64 mmol/mol) to estimated average glucose 183 mg/dL (95% CI 147–217) or 10.2 mmol/L (95% CI 8.1–12.1).
Table 6.1 maps A1C 9% (75 mmol/mol) to estimated average glucose 212 mg/dL (95% CI 170–249) or 11.8 mmol/L (95% CI 9.4–13.9).
Table 6.1 maps A1C 10% (86 mmol/mol) to estimated average glucose 240 mg/dL (95% CI 193–282) or 13.4 mmol/L (95% CI 10.7–15.7).
Table 6.1 maps A1C 11% (97 mmol/mol) to estimated average glucose 269 mg/dL (95% CI 217–314) or 14.9 mmol/L (95% CI 12.0–17.5).
Table 6.1 maps A1C 12% (108 mmol/mol) to estimated average glucose 298 mg/dL (95% CI 240–347) or 16.5 mmol/L (95% CI 13.3–19.3).

The ADAG estimates in Table 6.1 are based on approximately 2,700 glucose measurements over 3 months per A1C measurement in 507 adults with type 1 diabetes, type 2 diabetes, or no diabetes; the A1C–average glucose correlation was r=0.92.
Table 6.1 is based on a single 2008 ADAG study using an older intermittently worn CGM system plus capillary glucose, so generalizability to modern CGM-derived mean glucose is uncertain.
A 10–14 day CGM assessment with at least 70% active wear can be used to assess glycemic status and guide clinical management.
Table 6.2 CGM goal for Wear time: At least 14 days of wear for pattern management.
Table 6.2 CGM goal for Active percentage time: At least 70% active time out of 14 days.
Table 6.2 CGM goal for Glucose coefficient of variation: ≤36%.
Table 6.2 CGM goal for TAR >250 mg/dL: <5% for most adults; <10% for older adults with complex/intermediate health.
Table 6.2 CGM goal for TAR >180 mg/dL: <25% for most adults; <50% for older adults with complex/intermediate health.
Table 6.2 CGM goal for TIR 70–180 mg/dL: >70% for most adults; >50% for older adults with complex/intermediate health.
Table 6.2 CGM goal for TBR <70 mg/dL: <4% for most adults; <1% for older adults with complex/intermediate health.
Table 6.2 CGM goal for TBR <54 mg/dL: <1%.

Glycemic goals and evidence.statement: Table 6.3 target for many nonpregnant adults: A1C <7.0% (<53 mmol/mol).
Table 6.3 target for many nonpregnant adults: Preprandial capillary plasma glucose 80–130 mg/dL (4.4–7.2 mmol/L).
Table 6.3 target for many nonpregnant adults: Peak postprandial capillary plasma glucose <180 mg/dL (<10.0 mmol/L).
Recommendation 6.3a: An A1C goal below 7% (<53 mmol/mol) is appropriate for many nonpregnant adults without severe hypoglycemia or hypoglycemia affecting health or quality of life.
Recommendation 6.3b: A TIR goal above 70% is appropriate for many nonpregnant adults using CGM.
Recommendation 6.3c: For CGM users, target TBR below 70 mg/dL to less than 4%, or less than 1% for older adults.
Recommendation 6.3c: For CGM users, target TBR below 54 mg/dL to less than 1%.
Recommendation 6.3c: Deintensify or modify therapy when CGM hypoglycemia goals are not met.
Recommendation 6.4: A lower A1C goal, such as below 6.5%, may be appropriate when health and function are good and treatment risks and burdens are low.
Recommendation 6.5: Less stringent glycemic goals may be appropriate with significant cognitive/functional limitations, frailty, severe comorbidities, or when treatment harms exceed benefits.
Recommendation 6.6: Deintensify insulin, sulfonylureas, or meglitinides, or switch to a lower-hypoglycemia-risk class, for people at high hypoglycemia risk within individualized glycemic goals.
Recommendation 6.7: Deintensify diabetes medications when treatment harms or burdens may exceed benefits, within individualized glycemic goals.
Recommendation 6.8: Reassess glycemic goals using the individualized criteria in Figure 6.1.
Recommendation 6.9: Set a glycemic goal during clinical consultations to improve outcomes.
Figure 6.1 framework for Good health/function and low treatment risks/burdens: A1C <6.5%.
Figure 6.1 framework for Most adults: A1C <7.0%; TIR >70%; TBR <70 mg/dL <4%; TBR <54 mg/dL <1%; TAR >180 mg/dL <25%; TAR >250 mg/dL <5%.
Figure 6.1 framework for Healthy older adults: A1C <7.5%.
Figure 6.1 framework for Older adults with complex/intermediate health: A1C <8.0%; TIR >50%; TBR <70 mg/dL <1%; TBR <54 mg/dL <1%; TAR >180 mg/dL <50%; TAR >250 mg/dL <10%.
Figure 6.1 framework for Older adults with very complex/poor health or adults with limited life expectancy: No A1C goal; TBR <70 mg/dL <1%; TBR <54 mg/dL <1%; avoid symptomatic hyperglycemia.

Figure 6.1 favors more stringent goals with shorter diabetes duration, lower hypoglycemia risk, lower treatment risks/burdens, pharmacotherapy with nonglycemic cardiovascular/kidney/weight benefits, no cardiovascular complications, and few/minor comorbidities; opposite factors favor less stringent goals.
Figure 6.1 is intended as a shared-decision framework rather than a rigid rule; goals should avoid symptomatic hypoglycemia and hyperglycemia and account for available resources and support systems.

The guideline reports that DCCT intensive glycemic management (mean A1C about 7%) versus standard management (mean A1C about 9%) in type 1 diabetes reduced development/progression of microvascular complications by 50–76%.
The guideline reports that EDIC follow-up showed persistence of DCCT microvascular benefits over two decades after between-group glycemic separation disappeared.

The guideline reports that Kumamoto and UKPDS achieved mean A1C 7.1% versus 9.4% and 7.0% versus 7.9%, respectively, and found lower microvascular complication rates in their intensive-treatment arms.
At the end of intervention, DCCT, UKPDS, ACCORD, ADVANCE, and VADT did not demonstrate a significant reduction in composite cardiovascular events from intensive glycemic management.

An individual-participant-data meta-analysis of UKPDS, ACCORD, ADVANCE, and VADT reported fewer myocardial infarctions and major cardiovascular events with intensive glycemic management but no difference in stroke, heart failure, or mortality.
The guideline reports a 57% lower risk of nonfatal myocardial infarction, nonfatal stroke, or cardiovascular death in EDIC participants previously assigned to intensive versus standard DCCT therapy.
The guideline reports that the cardiovascular benefit associated with prior intensive DCCT management persisted for 30 years and was associated with a 32% reduction in cardiovascular disease events.
The chapter reports that multiple trials have demonstrated successful and safe deintensification of diabetes treatment.

Hypoglycemia assessment, prevention, and.statement: Recommendation 6.10: Review hypoglycemia history at every clinical encounter for all people at risk and evaluate events as indicated.
Recommendation 6.11: Screen people at risk for impaired hypoglycemia awareness at least annually and when clinically appropriate.
Recommendation 6.11: Refer people with impaired hypoglycemia awareness to a trained health professional for evidence-based intervention to improve awareness.
Recommendation 6.12: Screen people at high risk or with severe/frequent hypoglycemia for fear of hypoglycemia at least annually and when clinically appropriate.
Recommendation 6.12: Refer people with fear of hypoglycemia for evidence-based intervention by a trained health professional.
Recommendation 6.13: Consider hypoglycemia risk when selecting diabetes medications and glycemic goals.
Recommendation 6.14: CGM is beneficial and recommended for people at high risk for hypoglycemia.
Recommendation 6.15: Use glucose as the preferred treatment for a conscious person with glucose below 70 mg/dL, although any carbohydrate containing glucose may be used.
Recommendation 6.15: Avoid foods or beverages high in fat and/or protein for initial hypoglycemia treatment.
Recommendation 6.15: Recheck after 15 minutes and repeat treatment if hypoglycemia persists.
Recommendation 6.16: Prescribe glucagon for all people taking insulin or at high risk for hypoglycemia.
Recommendation 6.16: Educate family, caregivers, school personnel, and other support persons about glucagon location and administration.
Recommendation 6.16: Prefer glucagon preparations that do not require reconstitution.
Recommendation 6.17: First aid kits should include oral glucose for hypoglycemia treatment.

Recommendation 6.18: All people taking insulin or otherwise at risk for hypoglycemia should receive structured education on hypoglycemia prevention and treatment, with ongoing education for those experiencing events.
Recommendation 6.19: One or more level 2 or level 3 hypoglycemia episodes should prompt treatment-plan reevaluation, including deintensification or medication switching when appropriate.
Recommendation 6.20: Regularly assess cognitive function and increase hypoglycemia vigilance when cognition is impaired or declining.
Table 6.4 defines Level 1 hypoglycemia as Glucose <70 mg/dL (<3.9 mmol/L) and ≥54 mg/dL (≥3.0 mmol/L).
Table 6.4 defines Level 2 hypoglycemia as Glucose <54 mg/dL (<3.0 mmol/L).
Table 6.4 defines Level 3 hypoglycemia as Severe event with altered mental and/or physical status requiring assistance for treatment, irrespective of glucose level.

Recurrent level 2 and/or level 3 hypoglycemia is an urgent medical issue requiring treatment-plan adjustment, behavioral intervention, diabetes self-management education/support, and appropriate technology.

Claims-based epidemiologic studies miss most level 1 and level 2 hypoglycemia and substantially underestimate level 3 hypoglycemia, even though they document substantial hypoglycemia-related hospital utilization.

People treated with insulin, sulfonylureas, or meglitinides are considered at risk for clinically significant hypoglycemia; high risk is defined by at least one major risk factor or multiple other risk factors using clinical judgment.

Table 6.5 Major clinical/biological risk factors: recent level 2/3 hypoglycemia within 3–6 months; intensive insulin therapy; impaired awareness; kidney failure; cognitive impairment/dementia; history of metabolic surgery.

Table 6.5 Other clinical/biological risk factors: multiple recent level 1 episodes; basal insulin; age ≥75 years; female sex; high glycemic variability; polypharmacy; CVD; CKD; neuropathy; retinopathy; major depressive disorder; severe mental illness; gastroparesis; beta-blocker therapy.
Table 6.5 Major social/cultural/economic risk factors: food insecurity; low-income status; housing insecurity; religious/cultural fasting; underinsurance.
Table 6.5 Other social/cultural/economic risk factors: low health literacy; alcohol or substance use disorder.
Among people at risk for hypoglycemia, prior hypoglycemic events—especially level 2 or 3 events—are identified as the strongest predictors of recurrence.
Impaired hypoglycemia awareness is described as dramatically increasing the risk of level 3 hypoglycemia.

Hypoglycemia assessment, prevention, and.statement: Table 6.7 minimum prevention schedule: Training to improve hypoglycemia awareness — initial and annual when impaired awareness is detected.

Evidence-based awareness-training programs are described as reducing hypoglycemia and improving quality of life in type 1 diabetes with impaired awareness, but the cited programs are not currently available for routine clinical use.

Several weeks of hypoglycemia avoidance, often using temporary relaxation of glycemic goals, can improve counterregulation and awareness in many people with impaired hypoglycemia awareness and recurrent events.

Intercurrent illness and hyperglycemic c.statement: During illness or other stressful events, clinicians should consider more frequent glucose monitoring and, for ketosis-prone people, urine or blood ketone monitoring, while reevaluating diabetes treatment.
Consider holding metformin and SGLT2 inhibitors when oral intake cannot be maintained or acute kidney injury is a concern.
Hold thiazolidinediones and reassess reinitiation individually during heart-failure exacerbation or other hypervolemic states.

Because sulfonylureas can interact with fluoroquinolones, clarithromycin, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, metronidazole, and fluconazole to increase hypoglycemia risk, consider temporarily reducing or stopping the sulfonylurea when these antimicrobials are prescribed.
Recommendation 6.21: Review history of diabetic ketoacidosis and hyperglycemic hyperosmolar state at every encounter for all people at risk.

Recommendation 6.22: Provide structured education on recognition, prevention, and management of hyperglycemic crisis to all people with type 1 diabetes, people with type 2 diabetes who have experienced a crisis, and people at high risk.
DKA and HHS are described as serious, acute, life-threatening hyperglycemic emergencies whose rates have increased over the past decade in both type 1 and type 2 diabetes.
The chapter focuses on risk factors, prevention, and outpatient management of DKA/HHS; detailed diagnosis, presentation, and inpatient management are delegated to Standards section 16.
The guideline reports that DKA risk in people with type 1 diabetes using SGLT2 inhibitors can be 5–17 times higher than in nonusers.
The guideline reports that fasting beta-hydroxybutyrate ≥0.8 mmol/L in SGLT2-inhibitor trials of adults with type 1 diabetes was associated with a 3.2-fold higher risk of DKA in the following month.
In people with type 2 diabetes treated with SGLT2 inhibitors, the chapter reports DKA incidence of 0.6–4.9 events per 1,000 patient-years.

The guideline reports that a meta-analysis of four randomized trials found a relative risk of DKA of 2.46 (95% CI 1.16–5.21) with SGLT2 inhibitors versus placebo or active comparator in type 2 diabetes.
The guideline reports that a meta-analysis of five observational studies found a relative risk of DKA of 1.74 (95% CI 1.07–2.83) with SGLT2-inhibitor exposure in type 2 diabetes.
The guideline reports that up to 2% of pregnancies with pregestational diabetes are complicated by DKA, while DKA incidence in gestational diabetes is below 0.1%.
Pregnant people may present with euglycemic DKA at glucose below 200 mg/dL (11.1 mmol/L).
The guideline reports that a 6-month randomized trial found blood ketone monitoring reduced hospitalization/emergency-room management by approximately 50% compared with urine ketone monitoring.

Mild DKA may be managed with frequent glucose/ketone monitoring, noncaloric hydration, and subcutaneous insulin only when the person is hemodynamically and cognitively intact, can tolerate oral hydration, and can self-administer insulin; worsening symptoms, ongoing emesis, failure of glucose/ketones to improve, or altered mental status require immediate medical care.
Suspected HHS should be evaluated and treated in the inpatient setting because HHS is typically associated with marked volume depletion and an acute precipitating illness.

Table 6.8 lists hyperglycemic-crisis risk factors including type 1 diabetes/absolute insulin deficiency; younger age; prior hyperglycemic crisis; prior hypoglycemic crisis; other diabetes complications; other chronic health conditions, particularly in type 2 diabetes; behavioral health conditions such as depression, bipolar disorder, or eating disorders; alcohol/substance use; high A1C; insulin rationing; SGLT2/SGLT1/2 inhibitor use; adverse social determinants of health.
The chapter notes that a substantial proportion of people hospitalized with DKA experience recurrent episodes, supporting active identification of triggers and recurrence prevention.

People who have experienced DKA or HHS should be screened for social determinants that impede access to insulin, glucose-lowering medications, glucose monitoring, or insulin-delivery equipment and referred to appropriate health/community services.
Access to CGM may decrease DKA recurrence.
